items.name: para_hypertension
items.text: This randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial enrolled adults with stage 1 hypertension who were not taking any antihypertensive medication. Participants were allocated to a low-dose combination tablet or to placebo and followed for twelve months, with home blood pressure measured twice daily. The primary outcome was the change in mean systolic pressure from baseline to the final visit. Secondary outcomes included the proportion reaching a target below 130/80 mmHg, changes in estimated glomerular filtration rate, and the incidence of dizziness, cough and peripheral oedema. Analysis followed the intention-to-treat principle, and missing values were handled with multiple imputation under a missing-at-random assumption. Prespecified subgroup analyses examined age, sex, baseline body mass index and diabetes status, and an independent committee reviewed all serious adverse events without knowledge of treatment allocation until the database was locked.

items.name: para_cohort
items.text: We followed a population-based cohort of women aged 50 to 69 years who attended organised breast screening, linking attendance records to cancer registry and death certificate data. Exposure was defined as regular attendance, meaning at least three of the last four invitations were accepted. We estimated hazard ratios for breast cancer mortality with Cox models adjusted for deprivation score, parity, use of hormone therapy and body mass index. Lead-time and length-time bias were examined in sensitivity analyses, and overdiagnosis was estimated from the excess incidence in the screened group relative to an unscreened comparison cohort over a fifteen-year horizon. Results were broadly consistent across strata of age and baseline risk. The authors caution that residual confounding by health-seeking behaviour cannot be excluded, because women who attend regularly may differ from non-attenders in ways that are not captured by routinely collected registry variables.

items.name: para_review
items.text: A systematic review of exercise interventions for chronic low back pain searched five databases from inception and screened records in duplicate. Eligible trials compared supervised exercise with usual care, advice or no treatment in adults with pain lasting more than twelve weeks. Two reviewers extracted data and assessed risk of bias with a standard tool, and certainty of evidence was graded for each outcome. Random-effects meta-analysis showed a small to moderate reduction in pain intensity at the end of treatment, with substantial heterogeneity that was only partly explained by session frequency. Effects on disability were smaller, and few trials reported adverse events or follow-up beyond one year, which limits conclusions about durability. The review protocol was registered in advance, and deviations from it are listed; a funnel plot suggested possible small-study effects, so the pooled estimate may be somewhat optimistic.

items.name: para_qualitative
items.text: Semi-structured interviews were conducted with twenty-two general practitioners working in rural and remote settings to explore how they decide when to refer patients with suspected dementia to a specialist memory clinic. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Three themes were developed: uncertainty about the value of an early diagnosis, the practical burden of travelling long distances for assessment, and the central role of family carers in noticing change. Participants described relying on a long relationship with the patient rather than on formal cognitive tests, and asked for shared care models with telehealth support from specialists. Several described feeling professionally isolated when a referral was declined, and suggested that clearer criteria and faster feedback letters would make the pathway easier to trust for both clinicians and families.
